scope: Lecture 19, Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation
intro: Twenty patients. Read the pH, find the primary disorder, judge the compensation and, for a metabolic acidosis, work out the anion gap, then name the cause. Every value comes with its normal range.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.vignette: A 24-year-old man is brought in after friends found him very drowsy at home. He had taken several of a relative's prescription opioid pain pills. He is breathing slowly and shallowly. He has no lung or chest wall disease.

steps.label: pH
steps.prompt: What does the pH show?

options.e: Only a narrow pH range, 6.9 to 7.8, is compatible with life. A pH of 7.23 is abnormal but inside that range, so it is acidosis to be explained, not an unsurvivable value. Tell: this label marks the extremes of pH, not its direction.
Correct. The pH of 7.23 is below 7.35, outside the normal 7.35 to 7.45, so this is acidosis. The next step is to find which value, carbon dioxide or bicarbonate, is pushing the pH down.
A normal arterial pH is 7.35 to 7.45, and 7.23 is below it, so the pH is abnormal: acidosis. Tell: the pH is read against its own range before carbon dioxide or bicarbonate.
Alkalosis means a pH above 7.45. This pH is 7.23, below 7.35, so the blood is on the acid side. Tell: below the normal range is acidosis, above it is alkalosis; read the direction first.

walk: Compare the pH with its normal range, 7.35 to 7.45.
7.23 is below 7.35.
So the blood shows acidosis.
steps.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 17, 18, 19

steps.label: Primary disorder
steps.prompt: Which primary disorder explains the pH?

options.e: Metabolic acidosis needs a bicarbonate below 22. Here it is 25, inside 22 to 26, so it did not lower the pH; the high carbon dioxide of 62 did. Tell: in metabolic acidosis bicarbonate falls with the pH.
Metabolic alkalosis raises the pH above 7.45, and this pH is 7.23, acidosis. Its bicarbonate of 25 is not high either. Tell: in metabolic alkalosis bicarbonate and pH both rise.

Correct. The pH of 7.23 is low, and the carbon dioxide of 62 is above 45: retained carbon dioxide lowers the pH, so the problem is respiratory. The bicarbonate of 25 is still inside 22 to 26, so it does not explain the low pH.
Respiratory alkalosis raises the pH above 7.45, and this pH is 7.23, acidosis. Its carbon dioxide of 62 is not low either. Tell: the pH sets the direction before anything else.

walk: pH 7.23: acidosis.
Carbon dioxide 62 (normal 35 to 45): high, and a high carbon dioxide lowers the pH.
Bicarbonate 25 (normal 22 to 26): normal, and a normal bicarbonate does not move the pH.
The value that moves the pH the way it actually went is the carbon dioxide, so the primary disorder is respiratory acidosis.
steps.cite: Acid Base Balance and Blood Gas Interpretation mbf2026sc.pptx, Slides 27, 30, 31, 33, 50, 51, 52, 53

steps.label: Compensation
steps.prompt: How is the body compensating?

options.e: Correct. The bicarbonate of 25 is still inside 22 to 26, so the kidneys have not changed it yet. High carbon dioxide, low pH and a normal bicarbonate is the acute pattern; renal compensation takes days to build.
Kidneys raising bicarbonate would show a bicarbonate above 26. Here the bicarbonate is 25, still inside 22 to 26, so the kidneys have not responded yet. Tell: renal compensation takes days to appear.

Kidneys lowering bicarbonate would push the pH further the wrong way. In respiratory acidosis the kidneys offset the change by moving bicarbonate the same way as carbon dioxide; here bicarbonate is 25, inside 22 to 26. Tell: compensation always pulls the pH back toward normal.

The lungs are the source of this problem: the carbon dioxide of 62 is high because of how the patient is breathing. A respiratory disorder is compensated by the kidneys, through bicarbonate. Tell: the system that compensates is the one that is not the cause.

walk: Primary disorder: respiratory acidosis.
A respiratory disorder is compensated by the kidneys, which move bicarbonate the same way as carbon dioxide (up in acidosis, down in alkalosis), over days.
Bicarbonate here: 25 against 22 to 26, normal.
So: no compensation yet.

steps.label: Oxygen delivery
steps.prompt: How does this pH change hemoglobin's hold on oxygen?

options.t: Right shift: oxygen released more easily
options.e: Correct. The pH of 7.23 is acidic, and acidosis shifts the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve to the right: oxygen is released more easily from hemoglobin.

options.t: Left shift: oxygen held more tightly
options.e: A left shift, with oxygen held more tightly, is what alkalosis does. This pH of 7.23 is acidic, which shifts the curve right. Tell: a low pH shifts right and lets oxygen go.

options.t: Right shift: oxygen held more tightly
options.e: A right shift lowers hemoglobin's hold on oxygen; it does not tighten it. Acidosis, like this pH of 7.23, shifts the curve right so oxygen is released more easily. Tell: right shift means release.

options.t: Left shift: oxygen released more easily
options.e: A left shift tightens hemoglobin's hold, so oxygen is released less easily, and a left shift comes from alkalosis, not this acidic pH of 7.23. Tell: acid shifts right.

walk: pH 7.23: acidosis.
Acidosis (low pH) shifts the curve right: oxygen is released more easily.
Alkalosis (high pH) shifts the curve left: oxygen is held more tightly.
So: right shift: oxygen released more easily.

steps.label: Cause
steps.prompt: Which cause best fits this patient?

options.e: Kyphoscoliosis is a chest wall deformity that causes respiratory acidosis slowly, with time for renal compensation. He has no chest wall disease, and the normal bicarbonate says this began recently. Tell: chest wall disease is a long-standing cause.
Pulmonary emboli are counted among the causes of a low carbon dioxide, and his carbon dioxide is 62, high, with slow breathing. Tell: a cause of a low carbon dioxide does not fit a high one.

Emphysema is obstructive lung disease that raises carbon dioxide over years, and the kidneys then raise bicarbonate. He has no lung disease, and his bicarbonate of 25 is still normal. Tell: a long-standing cause comes with a raised bicarbonate.

Correct. Opioids are among the drugs that depress breathing and cause acute respiratory acidosis: his carbon dioxide of 62 is high while his bicarbonate of 25 is still normal, the acute pattern. He took opioid pills and is breathing slowly and shallowly.

walk: The gas is an acute respiratory acidosis: high carbon dioxide, bicarbonate not yet raised.
Acute respiratory acidosis comes from respiratory depression; drugs such as opioids, barbiturates and anesthetics are the recognized causes.
He took opioid pills, breathes slowly, and has no long-standing lung or chest wall disease.
So: opioid overdose.

Correct. The pH of 7.48 is high, and the bicarbonate of 33 is above 26: extra bicarbonate raises the pH, so the problem is metabolic. The carbon dioxide of 46 is high too, but a high carbon dioxide would lower the pH, so it did not cause the alkalosis.

options.e: Lungs lowering carbon dioxide would push the pH further the wrong way. In metabolic alkalosis the lungs offset the change by moving carbon dioxide the same way as bicarbonate; here carbon dioxide is 46, above 45. Tell: compensation always pulls the pH back toward normal.
Correct. The carbon dioxide of 46 is above 45: slower breathing retains carbon dioxide to offset the high bicarbonate. Respiratory compensation for a metabolic disorder works within minutes to hours.

The carbon dioxide of 46 is outside its normal 35 to 45, moved in the direction that pulls the pH back toward normal, so compensation has begun. Tell: only a normal carbon dioxide would mean none yet.

Carbon dioxide here: 46 against 35 to 45, high.
So: lungs raising carbon dioxide.

options.e: Correct. Excessive bicarbonate administration is the recognized base-gain cause of metabolic alkalosis. Repeated intravenous sodium bicarbonate during her resuscitation explains her bicarbonate of 33.
Vomiting is an acid-loss cause, and she has not vomited. Tell: acid loss needs a route, vomiting or suction; base gain needs bicarbonate given.
Lactic acidosis is an acid-gain cause of metabolic acidosis. Today her pH is 7.48 and her bicarbonate 33, an alkalosis. Tell: read today's gas, not the arrest.
Nasogastric suction loses gastric acid, but she has no tube draining her stomach. Tell: no tube, no suction loss.

cases.title: Case 20
cases.vignette: An 18-year-old woman with asthma has wheezed badly for six hours despite her inhaler. She is now tiring and can speak only a few words at a time. She has no other lung or chest wall disease.

steps.label: pH
steps.prompt: What does the pH show?

options.e: Alkalosis means a pH above 7.45. This pH is 7.30, below 7.35, so the blood is on the acid side. Tell: below the normal range is acidosis, above it is alkalosis; read the direction first.
Correct. The pH of 7.30 is below 7.35, outside the normal 7.35 to 7.45, so this is acidosis. The next step is to find which value, carbon dioxide or bicarbonate, is pushing the pH down.
A normal arterial pH is 7.35 to 7.45, and 7.30 is below it, so the pH is abnormal: acidosis. Tell: the pH is read against its own range before carbon dioxide or bicarbonate.

Only a narrow pH range, 6.9 to 7.8, is compatible with life. A pH of 7.30 is abnormal but inside that range, so it is acidosis to be explained, not an unsurvivable value. Tell: this label marks the extremes of pH, not its direction.

walk: Compare the pH with its normal range, 7.35 to 7.45.
7.30 is below 7.35.
So the blood shows acidosis.

Correct. The pH of 7.30 is low, and the carbon dioxide of 52 is above 45: retained carbon dioxide lowers the pH, so the problem is respiratory. The bicarbonate of 25 is still inside 22 to 26, so it does not explain the low pH.
Respiratory alkalosis raises the pH above 7.45, and this pH is 7.30, acidosis. Its carbon dioxide of 52 is not low either. Tell: the pH sets the direction before anything else.

options.e: Correct. The bicarbonate of 25 is still inside 22 to 26, so the kidneys have not changed it yet. High carbon dioxide, low pH and a normal bicarbonate is the acute pattern; renal compensation takes days to build.

The lungs are the source of this problem: the carbon dioxide of 52 is high because of how the patient is breathing. A respiratory disorder is compensated by the kidneys, through bicarbonate. Tell: the system that compensates is the one that is not the cause.

steps.label: Cause
steps.prompt: Which cause best fits this patient?

options.e: Kyphoscoliosis is a chest wall cause that acts over years, and she has no chest wall disease. Tell: a six-hour illness with a normal bicarbonate is acute.
Anxiety speeds breathing and lowers carbon dioxide. Her carbon dioxide is 52, high. Tell: anxiety is a respiratory alkalosis cause.
Emphysema raises carbon dioxide over years, with a renal rise in bicarbonate. She is 18, has no other lung disease, and her bicarbonate of 25 is normal. Tell: chronic causes raise the bicarbonate.

Correct. Asthma is a recognized airway obstruction cause of a raised carbon dioxide. Six hours of severe wheezing have tired her, so carbon dioxide has climbed to 52, and the bicarbonate of 25 shows there has been no time for renal compensation.

walk: The gas is an acute respiratory acidosis: carbon dioxide high, bicarbonate normal.
Airway obstruction, including asthma, raises carbon dioxide.
Six hours of severe wheezing in a known asthmatic, now tiring.
So: asthma.
